title: Jeff Nippard & Minimalism: Working Hard or Hardly Working?
summary: NH critiques Jeff Nippard's minimalism framing and marketing for his paid 'Essentials' programs, then reviews the programs themselves. He argues more training yields more results as long as fatigue is managed, that minimalism suits novices, that 'junk volume' is relative to the individual, and concludes the programs are not truly minimalist but efficient, well-built and worth buying for those set on buying a program.
claims: Maximalism defined as spending as much time as needed to maximize progress is a fair definition
Claiming 1 hour gets 98% of the gains of 2 hours is misleading; he believes the second hour can add roughly 20-30% for some individuals
Training more always produces more results as long as fatigue is taken into account; actually hurting gains by overdoing it is rare
You can get about 80% of the results from roughly 60-70% of a program, because the first hour carries most of the gains
Pyramid of priority: put the most important lifts at the top of the session, so cutting the bottom loses only about 10-20% of gains
Minimalism benefits novices the most because they need the least work to grow; for an advanced lifter like him it would be shooting himself in the foot
He trains up to three hours in the gym, not because he enjoys it but because volume matters for him
Fitness tailored to the lowest common denominator degrades standards; people who say they have no time usually have time for Netflix
Optimal training is case-by-case: a three-hour workout that you hate and abandon is worse than a shorter one you follow
Branding a short program as minimalism makes it sound smart and lets people feel good about training less
Jeff's marketing is 'normie baiting' rather than malicious: lure beginners with short workouts, they fall in love with training and later scale up
Long, high-set programs burn beginners out; lacking work capacity, they sandbag to survive and produce junk volume
For a novice two hard sets can tire a muscle enough to grow, so three hours in the gym is wasted
Novices should start around 45 minutes to an hour and lengthen sessions as they progress
Data cited: one set per week gives about 64% of the gains for novices; that percentage falls as you become advanced, maybe to around 30%, which is why added volume makes sense
Using Dorian Yates to sell a natural program is disingenuous; his physique came from PEDs, not HIT
There is nothing magical about one set to beyond failure; HIT has been debunked by naturals; Mentzer was brilliant but wrong on things like EZ curls
Jeff Alberts is an advanced natural who uses only about 4 hard sets per week with a small exercise pool; it may maintain rather than maximize muscle
Most lifters do 12-20 sets per week per muscle; around 10 can work for intermediates
Minimalism is mostly a strength practice: maintaining or building strength needs far fewer sets than building muscle; hypertrophy is a game of volume
True HIT is one set to failure every 6-8 days; the 'HIT police' redefine HIT whenever it fails, which is intellectually dishonest
Terms defined by absence (minimalism) only exist in opposition to something else
Junk volume is relative: it is the point where additional work yields too little based on your muscular endurance; one man's junk volume is another's treasure
Calling every set after the top set junk volume would logically mean only one set should ever be done, i.e. Mentzer was right
Dogmatic claims like more than five minutes of ab work a day is junk volume ignore training age; he has trained abs for 10 years and needs more
Adding a second working set after warming up only costs about 3-4 minutes, so do not be dogmatic about set counts
Drop sets are ironic in a time-saving program because a drop after a heavy set is done pre-fatigued and is lower-quality volume than another straight set
With only one top set, all intensity is concentrated into it and you go to failure, raising injury risk; multiple sets allow reps in reserve
70-80% of gym time is spent resting; cut time with supersets, even of unrelated muscles (e.g. lunges with skull crushers, lateral raises with calf raises), rather than cutting hard sets
Upper-body days should be long and lower-body days short: lower lifts are more energy-costly and hit more muscle per lift, while upper needs more isolation
The Essentials programs are Jeff's best: excellent exercise selection, rotations, two substitution options per lift, proper pyramid ordering; efficient, not minimalist
You should ideally make your own program, but if you buy one, these (about 40 pages each) are worth it and can be scaled up with more sets for years
A minimalist refuses to do more even knowing it helps; a maximalist refuses to do less even knowing it helps; do what works and is convenient
